p: The Hebrew says twenty pieces of silver; the Greek says twenty pieces of gold.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Samaritan Pentateuch; Targums; KJV, BSB
Septuagint (εἴκοσι χρυσῶν, "twenty gold pieces")

why: Silver was the ordinary money of slave sales in the ancient Near East, and the Hebrew, Samaritan and Aramaic texts agree. The Greek translators may have raised the price to suit the value of a slave in their own day, or to honor Joseph.
b: Later retellings also speak of gold: the Testament of Gad (2:3) gives thirty pieces of gold. I have not checked that passage against a critical edition. The Greek reading bears on the note about slave prices on this verse.

p: The standard Hebrew text spells the traders "Medanites" here; other witnesses have "Midianites."

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint, Latin Vulgate, Syriac; most English versions
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)

why: The two words differ by one letter (yod). The traders were called Midianites a few verses earlier (37:28), and the other ancient witnesses all read Midianites. Medan and Midian were both sons of Abraham by Keturah (25:2), so the Masoretic spelling may be a copying slip or a by-form of the same name. The meaning is the same either way.

t: "All the storehouses" or "all that was in them"?
p: The Hebrew says Joseph opened "all that was in them." The Greek says "all the granaries."

readings.w: Septuagint (pantas tous sitobolōnas, "all the granaries"); the sense supplied by the KJV and most English versions
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: Joseph opened all that was in them
readings.plain: Joseph opened up everything that was in them

why: The Hebrew is very short, and "them" has no clear antecedent; it probably points back to the cities where the grain was stored (41:48). A word such as "storehouses" may have dropped out, or the Hebrew may simply be elliptical. The Greek translators, and most English versions, supply the sense. The meaning is not in doubt.

p: The Samaritan and Greek texts add a blessing spoken by Joseph.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); KJV, BSB
Samaritan Pentateuch; Septuagint (Εὐλογητὸς ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος τῷ θεῷ)
readings.en: and he said, Blessed be that man by God
readings.plain: He is still alive." And he said, "Blessed be that man by God."

why: The shorter Hebrew is followed. The added blessing fits Joseph's warmth and may be a scribe's expansion meant to give him a reply to his brothers' news.
b: I give this plus as it is reported in standard editions and commentaries; I could not check the Samaritan wording directly.

a: 'Why have you paid back evil for good?
t: Does the steward mention the cup?
p: The Greek adds a question: "Why have you stolen my silver cup?"

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Samaritan Pentateuch; KJV, BSB
readings.en: Why have you repaid evil for good?
readings.plain: 'Why have you paid back evil for good?

readings.w: Septuagint
readings.orig: ἵνα τί ἀνταπεδώκατε πονηρὰ ἀντὶ καλῶν; ἵνα τί ἐκλέψατέ μου τὸ κόνδυ τὸ ἀργυροῦν;
readings.en: Why have you repaid evil for good? Why have you stolen my silver cup?
readings.plain: 'Why have you paid back evil for good? Why have you stolen my silver cup?

why: In the Hebrew, the next verse says "This is what my master drinks from" without having named the cup, which is abrupt. The Greek smooths this by adding a question. Scribes and translators more often add clarifying words than remove them, so the shorter Hebrew is probably original.

p: Issachar's third son is "Iob" in the Hebrew of Genesis, but "Jashub" everywhere else.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); KJV "Job"
Samaritan Pentateuch; Septuagint (Iasoub); compare Numbers 26:24 and 1 Chronicles 7:1

why: Numbers 26:24 and 1 Chronicles 7:1 give the name as Jashub, and the Samaritan and Greek texts have that form here too. Iob may be a shortened form or a copying error in which a letter dropped out. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew of Genesis, but the person is almost certainly the same. Several other names in this list also differ slightly from Numbers 26 (for example Ziphion and Zephon in 46:16; Jemuel and Nemuel in 46:10).

a: In the land of Egypt, Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph. Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore them to him.
t: Joseph's grandsons in the Greek list
p: The Greek adds five of Joseph's descendants here, which is how its total reaches seventy-five (see 46:27).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.en: Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph in the land of Egypt
readings.plain: In the land of Egypt, Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph. Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore them to him.

readings.w: Septuagint
readings.orig: ἐγένοντο δὲ υἱοὶ Μανασση, οὓς ἔτεκεν αὐτῷ ἡ παλλακὴ ἡ Σύρα, τὸν Μαχιρ· Μαχιρ δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Γαλααδ. υἱοὶ δὲ Εφραιμ...
readings.en: adds: sons were born to Manasseh... Machir, and Machir fathered Galaad; the sons of Ephraim... Soutalaam and Taam; the sons of Soutalaam: Edem
readings.plain: In the land of Egypt, Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph. Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore them to him. Sons were born to Manasseh, whom his Aramean concubine bore to him: Machir. And Machir fathered Gilead. The sons of Ephraim, Manasseh's brother: Shuthelah and Tahan. And the son of Shuthelah: Edem.

why: The Greek list is longer because it includes Joseph's grandsons and a great-grandson, drawn from the family lists in Numbers 26:29–36 and 1 Chronicles 7:14–20. These men were born later, in Egypt, so most scholars see the Greek as an expansion that brings the list up to date. The Hebrew is followed here.
b: The added names match other lists: Machir and Gilead (Numbers 26:29; 1 Chronicles 7:14), Shuthelah and Tahan (Numbers 26:35). "Edem" corresponds to Eran in Numbers 26:36. See the next variant for how this changes the total.

a: With the two sons born to Joseph in Egypt, all the persons of the house of Jacob who came to Egypt numbered seventy.
p: The Hebrew counts seventy; the Greek counts seventy-five, the number Stephen gives in Acts 7:14.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Samaritan Pentateuch; Exodus 1:5 and Deuteronomy 10:22 in the Masoretic Text; Septuagint of Deuteronomy 10:22; Josephus (Antiquities 2.176–183)
readings.plain: With the two sons born to Joseph in Egypt, all the persons of the house of Jacob who came to Egypt numbered seventy.

readings.w: Septuagint; also the Greek of Exodus 1:5, and two Dead Sea Scrolls at Exodus 1:5 (4QExod-b, and 4QGen-Exod-a, which seems to read "and five souls"); Acts 7:14
readings.plain: With the nine sons born to Joseph in Egypt, all the persons of the house of Jacob who came to Egypt numbered seventy-five.

why: Both numbers are ancient. The Hebrew total of seventy fits the lists as they stand in the Hebrew (see the note at 46:15). The Greek reaches seventy-five by adding five descendants of Joseph in 46:20 and counting nine "sons" of Joseph. Stephen, speaking in Greek and quoting the Greek Bible, says "seventy-five persons" (Acts 7:14). The Dead Sea Scrolls show that seventy-five was also found in Hebrew copies of Exodus 1:5. As far as published lists show, no Qumran copy of Genesis 46:27 itself survives. The Greek Bible is not uniform either: its Deuteronomy 10:22 says seventy, and Josephus also counts seventy, while Philo (On the Migration of Abraham 199) comments on seventy-five.
b: Christian interpreters from Augustine on have discussed the difference. Some explain that Stephen followed the Greek text his hearers used; others suggest that the two totals count different groups (with or without Joseph's family, or including the wives). Either way, the difference shows that more than one form of the text circulated before the time of Jesus.

a: to point the way before him to Goshen
t: "Show the way" or "meet him at Heroonpolis"?
p: The Greek has Judah sent "to meet him at Heroonpolis, in the land of Rameses."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: to show [the way] before him to Goshen
readings.plain: to point the way before him to Goshen

readings.w: Septuagint
readings.orig: συναντῆσαι αὐτῷ καθ' Ἡρώων πόλιν εἰς γῆν Ραμεσση
readings.en: to meet him at Heroonpolis, into the land of Rameses
readings.plain: to meet him at Heroonpolis, in the land of Rameses

why: The Hebrew lehorot ("to direct, to show") is unusual here, and the Greek translators, working in Egypt, seem to have interpreted the verse with local knowledge, naming the city of Heroonpolis in the eastern Delta and the district of Rameses (47:11). The Samaritan Pentateuch is reported to read "to appear before him" (lehera'ot); I have not been able to check this reading directly. The Hebrew is followed as the harder and probably older text.

a: he moved them into the cities
t: Moved to the cities, or made slaves?
p: The Hebrew says Joseph moved the people into the cities; the Samaritan and Greek texts say he made them slaves.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); KJV
readings.en: he moved them to the cities
readings.plain: he moved them into the cities

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch; Septuagint; followed by many modern versions, including the BSB
readings.orig: הֶעֱבִיד אֹתוֹ לַעֲבָדִים / κατεδουλώσατο αὐτῷ εἰς παῖδας

why: The two Hebrew readings differ by one letter that looks very similar in Hebrew script (resh and dalet) and by the following word ("to cities" or "to slaves"). The Samaritan and Greek reading fits the context, where the people offer to become Pharaoh's slaves (47:19, 25), and many scholars prefer it. The Masoretic reading is the harder one and makes sense as a policy for distributing grain from the city stores (41:48). The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic Text but considers the other reading quite possibly original.
b: If the Samaritan and Greek reading is original, the people are not relocated but made serfs, which is how 47:25 describes their status in any case.

a: at the head of the bed
p: The same Hebrew letters can be read "bed" or "staff." Hebrews 11:21 follows the Greek: "the top of his staff."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (vowels added by Jewish scribes); Targums; KJV, BSB
readings.en: on the head of the bed
readings.plain: at the head of the bed

readings.w: Septuagint; quoted in Hebrews 11:21; Syriac Peshitta
readings.orig: ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου αὐτοῦ
readings.en: on the top of his staff
readings.plain: leaning on the top of his staff

why: Early Hebrew was written without vowels. The letters מטה can be mittah, "bed," or matteh, "staff." The Masoretic vowels give "bed," which fits 48:2 ("sat up on the bed") and 49:33. The Septuagint's "staff" is also possible, since Jacob had crossed the Jordan with his staff (32:10), and Hebrews 11:21 quotes the Greek. Both readings are old; the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew tradition.
b: The Latin Vulgate of Hebrews 11:21 says that Jacob "worshiped the top of his staff," a phrase later argued over in debates about honoring sacred objects. The Greek more naturally means that Jacob leaned on his own staff as he worshiped. Aquila and Symmachus, Greek versions made from the Hebrew, read "bed."

p: The Hebrew says they hamstrung an ox; other ancient versions say they tore down a wall, as the KJV does.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (שׁוֹר, shor); Septuagint (ἐνευροκόπησαν ταῦρον, "they hamstrung a bull"); BSB, ESV, NIV
Read as שׁוּר (shur), "wall": Targum Onkelos ("they destroyed the wall of the enemy"); Aquila and Symmachus; Latin Vulgate (suffoderunt murum); KJV "digged down a wall"

why: The consonants are the same; only the vowel differs. "Ox" matches the verb, which elsewhere means to cut an animal's tendons (Joshua 11:6), and it is the reading of the Hebrew and the Greek. "Wall" may be an attempt to fit the line to the sack of Shechem in Genesis 34, where the oxen were taken, not crippled.

t: "Until Shiloh comes": five ways to read it
p: The Hebrew letters can be read as a name, a place, "what belongs to him," or "tribute to him."

readings.w: Masoretic Text as vowelled (Leningrad Codex spells שילה; many manuscripts שילו); Samaritan Pentateuch (שלה); KJV, BSB
Same letters read as a place: some medieval Jewish commentators and many modern scholars

Read as shelloh, "which is his": Syriac Peshitta; the sense of Targum Onkelos ("until the Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs") and of Targums Neofiti and Pseudo-Jonathan ("until the time King Messiah comes"); compare the Dead Sea Scrolls commentary 4Q252 (1st century BC, an interpretation rather than a copy of Genesis): "until the Messiah of righteousness comes, the branch of David"; NIV
readings.en: until he comes to whom it belongs
readings.plain: until he comes to whom it belongs

readings.w: Septuagint (most manuscripts)
readings.orig: ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀποκείμενα αὐτῷ
readings.en: until the things stored up for him come
readings.plain: until what is stored up for him comes

readings.w: Repointed as shai loh, "tribute to him" (W. L. Moran, 1958); ESV, NRSV

why: No reading is certain. "Shiloh" as a personal name is found nowhere else, which is why many scholars look for another sense. "Which is his" fits Ezekiel 21:27, which seems to echo this verse ("until he comes whose right it is"), and it lies behind the ancient Jewish and Christian messianic readings. "Tribute to him" fits the parallel line about the obedience of the peoples. The town of Shiloh, where the tabernacle later stood (Joshua 18:1; 1 Samuel 1:3), is spelled the same way. The Plain English Translation keeps the letters as they stand and leaves the meaning open; see the note on "Shiloh."
b: Some manuscripts of the Septuagint read "until he comes for whom it is stored up," which agrees with the "which is his" reading. Justin Martyr knew both Greek forms (Dialogue with Trypho 120).

p: This goes with the variant on 49:20: one letter can end this verse or begin the next.

readings.w: Joining the first letter of 49:20 to this verse: Septuagint ("at their feet"); most modern versions
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); KJV "at the last"

why: The Hebrew line divides the letters so that 49:20 begins "From Asher." Moving the letter m back to the end of 49:19 gives "their heel," which completes the wordplay on Gad (raiders raid him, he raids their heel) and lets 49:20 begin simply "Asher," like the other sayings. The Plain English Translation follows this division; the two entries belong together.

p: This goes with the variant on 49:19: the Hebrew begins this verse "From Asher."

readings.w: Septuagint ("Asher, his bread is rich"); Latin Vulgate; Syriac Peshitta; most modern versions
Masoretic Text (מֵאָשֵׁר, me'asher); KJV "Out of Asher"

why: Every other saying in the poem begins with the tribe's name. The ancient versions begin "Asher," which suggests that the letter m belongs to the end of 49:19. The meaning changes very little. The two entries belong together.

p: A change of one vowel turns "from there" into "by the name of."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (מִשָּׁם, misham); KJV "from thence"
Read as מִשֵּׁם (mishem): Syriac Peshitta, as reported in the commentaries; BSB "in the name of"

why: The Hebrew is followed, though it is obscure. "By the name of the Shepherd" reads more smoothly, and some translations adopt it. I have not checked the Syriac directly.

p: The Hebrew reads "and with Shaddai"; other witnesses read "and El Shaddai," God Almighty.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
Samaritan Pentateuch, some Hebrew manuscripts, Septuagint and Syriac (as reported in the standard critical apparatus)

why: The difference is one letter: et ("with") or El ("God"). "El Shaddai" is the usual form of the name in Genesis (43:14; 48:3), and it makes a neat parallel with "the God of your father" in the line before. But the Masoretic reading also makes sense, and the meaning is the same: Joseph's blessing comes from the Almighty. I have relied on the standard critical apparatus for the list of witnesses.

a: than the blessings of the eternal mountains
p: Different vowels turn "my forefathers" into "the eternal mountains," which fits the next line.

readings.w: Septuagint ("of enduring mountains"); compare Deuteronomy 33:15 and Habakkuk 3:6; most modern versions
readings.plain: than the blessings of the eternal mountains

readings.w: Masoretic Text (vowels added by Jewish scribes); KJV
readings.en: my parents ("those who conceived me"), to the limit of...
readings.plain: than the blessings of my forefathers

why: The consonants can be read horai 'ad, "my progenitors, until," or harerei 'ad, "the eternal mountains." The second makes a natural pair with "the everlasting hills" in the next line, and Moses' blessing of Joseph has the same pair (Deuteronomy 33:15; compare Habakkuk 3:6). The Plain English Translation follows it, as most modern translations do. The Masoretic reading, "the blessings of your father are greater than the blessings of my ancestors," is also meaningful: Jacob's blessing on Joseph surpasses those he received from Abraham and Isaac.
